moves.title: Two researchers propose deadlines and forecast triggers for the loss and damage fund
moves.actor: Hemant Ojha, Australian National University and the Institute for Study and Development Worldwide, with Bhim Adhikari of Canada's International Development Research Centre
moves.place: Published from Sydney, addressed to the Antalya conference
moves.body: Writing three days before the conference opened, the two authors argued that the loss and damage fund's binding constraint is speed rather than size, and that its board calendar, consensus decision-making and case-by-case appraisal are the causes. They propose pre-agreed triggers releasing cash through regional risk pools, social protection systems and bodies such as the Pacific Resilience Facility; larger recovery grants over months and multi-year programmes for slow-onset losses including drought and displacement; hard deadlines of rapid finance within fourteen days of a declared sudden-onset disaster and recovery grant decisions within about ninety days of a request; public metrics on how long money takes to reach communities; and repositioning the fund as a coordinating hub working through regional funds and national institutions under shared standards. Their comparators are concrete: a regional pool and catastrophe bond due to pay Jamaica 242 million dollars within sixteen days of a hurricane, and a regional insurer paying Vanuatu within fourteen days of its 2024 earthquake, against the fund's own 57 days to set aside 21.6 million dollars for Nepal and no disbursement yet. One author's employer funded the cited research, which the article discloses.
moves.stated_rationale: That those who did least to heat the planet should not bear the cost of the damage, and that a fund which takes months to decide cannot discharge that obligation however much it holds.
moves.inference: The substance of this is the second independent arrival of the same design idea in a fortnight. On 22 October the director of a Swedish peace research institute's climate programme argued that climate security's problem is ownership rather than coordination, and proposed one accountable central body with a budget line plus pre-agreed finance released on forecast thresholds. These authors, from an entirely different literature — development research rather than peace research — reach the forecast-trigger half of that proposition independently and add deadlines, metrics and a hub-and-spoke architecture. When two unconnected research communities converge on releasing climate money by pre-agreed trigger rather than by committee, the idea has stopped being one institute's position and become the field's reform consensus. What it still lacks is any institution willing to surrender discretion, and the fund's own week-old evidence suggests why: the three governments that insisted its first allocation set no precedent are the ones whose aid budgets are under security-spending pressure, and a trigger is a precedent by construction.

moves.title: India fixes its conference position on finance and refuses conditional adaptation metrics
moves.actor: Bhupender Yadav, Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, India
moves.body: At a New Delhi briefing on 3 November the minister set out India's Antalya priorities. On finance: a decision to commence the climate finance work programme, with finance treated as a developed-country obligation under the agreement's finance article, predominantly public, concessional and not debt-creating. On adaptation: voluntary indicators under the global goal on adaptation so that they do not condition access to finance, and scaled-up adaptation finance as grants. On process: mitigation and the stocktake to stay party-driven, facilitative and non-punitive, the nationally determined character of pledges respected, no new top-down targets, carbon market participation voluntary, and presidency action-agenda initiatives kept out of the formal negotiations. India is reported as rejecting the host's electrification pledge and will coordinate with the Group of 77 and China, the like-minded developing countries and the Brazil, South Africa, India, China grouping.
moves.stated_rationale: Equity and differentiated responsibility, finance as an existing treaty obligation rather than a new pledge, and practical Global South solutions over new targets.
moves.inference: The adaptation half of this is the interesting half, and it is not the position a casual reader would predict. India is asking for more adaptation money and simultaneously insisting that the metric by which adaptation progress is measured must stay voluntary. The only reading in which those are consistent is that India expects the indicator set to become a gate — an eligibility test, an appraisal standard, a conditionality — and is legislating against that outcome three years before anyone has proposed it. Set this against the thing this publication has recorded about India all autumn: a state that executes six-figure pre-emptive evacuations, has just enlarged the fiscal instrument that pays for them, and attaches no security vocabulary to any of it. The same instinct is operating at the conference. India will take adaptation money and will not take an externally held yardstick for what it did with it, because the yardstick is the part that constrains sovereignty and the money is the part that does not. The parallel with its position on the science panel's timetable is exact.

roster_silences:
Worked this week, with the route named in each case, because an absence from a named route and an absence of output are different findings.

- **The American climate security institute.** Checked its own climate-change tag, which is the route that carried its last four items. Nothing since the European food security assessment of 29 October. Its homepage is reported as carrying a 2 November blog post on artificial intelligence under the centre's heading, credited to a different lab; that item does not appear on the climate tag and is not counted here as climate research. Eleven days.
- **The alliance's climate centre of excellence in Montreal.** Nothing. Twenty-four days after its own climate security summit of 15 and 16 October, neither host has published anything from it, against published recaps of the 2024 edition on 30 October 2024 and the 2025 edition on 15 October 2025. The contrast is now a month old.
- **The international military council.** Tenth consecutive week with nothing on its flagship annual report, and nothing from the Montreal meeting its secretary general was listed to speak at.
- **The Hague centre.** Its most recent climate-security research remains 15 July. One adjacent finding surfaced this week from the parliamentary record rather than from the centre: its own commentary on the Dutch defence climate strategy argues the strategy lacks a firm national anchor, clear operational steps and explicit choices, and that the test will be the action plan — and the defence committee asked the minister in September to respond to the centre's report by the end of that month. No response has been found.
- **The attribution network.** Nothing published inside the week. Its most recent event papers are a typhoon study of 28 October and a hurricane study of 15 October. No study of the Florida record, the Horn of Africa season or the European heat season.
- **The joint United Nations climate security unit.** Nothing found since 15 October, now three and a half weeks.
- **The small island states' alliance.** No new statement found; the most recent remains 21 September. In the week its member states' adaptation need was priced at 49 to 83 per cent coverable by the tripling they are negotiating for, that silence is the most surprising on this list.

Publishing this week: the Stockholm institute, which issued a climate, peace and security fact sheet on Somalia dated November, by two named researchers and a geospatial consultant with a Norwegian institute co-author. It identifies livelihood erosion, humanitarian deterioration and local resource conflict interacting with political fragmentation and continued fighting, notes the national drought emergency declared in November 2025 after four failed seasons, and carries the forecast of wetter-than-usual conditions and high flood risk in central and southern Somalia for this October-to-December season. The exact day of publication is not given on its page. This is the roster's only climate-security research output of the week and it is a country fact sheet, which says something about where the field's remaining institutional capacity is being spent.

active_trends.text: Removal of climate from security vehicles rather than only from language, and this week the trend acquired its first instance of the opposite motion. The Union's standing security committee co-signed a communique naming the adverse impacts of climate change as a driver of insecurity in the Sahel and committing to address them in the Lake Chad basin — a security vehicle acquiring the referent rather than losing it. The qualification is geographic. The same institution's internal resilience instrument, published nine days earlier, contains no security body at all. So the three forms this trend has tracked — deletion from instruments that bind, demotion to premise in instruments that buy, absence from instruments built in the civil-protection register — now need a fourth: presence in instruments that describe somebody else's territory. That is the cheapest form of all, because it commits nothing, and it is the only form in which the word is currently safe inside European security language.

Closed in the week ending 2026-10-25 and retained for the record, because the finding it recorded held for ten weeks: American adaptation survives federally only as emergency management. This week extends it with the cleanest single illustration it has had. A record daily rainfall broke an 89-year series on a Florida city, two people died, about 160 rescues were made, and the whole federal-facing response available was a state emergency declaration for seven counties opening the route to assistance. No pre-disaster instrument was invoked because the principal one no longer exists. The Indian observation recorded a fortnight ago stands alongside it: the same structure arrived at by a different route, funded through notified calamities and disaster funds, with no security vocabulary attached and, unlike the American case, working. Successor trend: where displaced capacity goes.

Security Council shift from climate security to natural resource governance, and now past it into something more specific. November's presidency chose a single signature event and it is a high-level open debate on emerging technologies and security. That is the second consecutive month in which this Council has given a discretionary slot to a technology framing, and the comparison that fixes its meaning is annual rather than monthly: in November 2025 this Council held a formal meeting titled climate and security, on the environmental impact of armed conflict and climate-driven security risks, with the political affairs department and the environment programme briefing. One year on, same month, the slot is technology. The resource-governance frame did not disappear, though. It reappeared on 6 November in the African Union and Union joint communique, condemning the illegal exploitation of natural resources in eastern Congo — after both sides had proposed and then dropped an agenda item on exactly that subject. The frame is now a conflict-economy frame that travels without an agenda item, which is a different thing from the resource-governance agenda this trend opened on.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments, and this week the mechanism inverted. The outgoing conference presidency published the two documents its own conference could not agree as decisions — a fossil fuel transition roadmap with a sequence running to 2033, and a deforestation roadmap — both explicitly non-negotiated, both outside the treaty regime by design, because that was the price of their existing at all. So the trend now has two directions. Obligations are being removed from instruments that bind, and ambition is being relocated into instruments that do not, and the second is presented as a success. The first fight at Antalya is over whether the cover decision may even cite the roadmap, which is the exact measure of what relocation costs: an instrument so voluntary that referring to it is contested.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment, and this week the pattern was visible in a budget debate rather than inferred from silence. The chamber debated the 2027 climate budget on 4 and 5 November and, on its own published summary of sixteen speakers, climate adaptation, water safety, defence and climate security did not appear. A correction also lands here: the infrastructure and water budget was debated on 28 and 29 October, not later in the autumn as this publication said, and its dominant subject was a 284 million euro cut to the freshwater line, with national co-financing for regional freshwater measures lapsing from 2027. Against that: the defence climate strategy of 3 July carries five million euros structural from 2027 with every further cost to be absorbed internally and an action plan now four months overdue, three documents are promised for December, and the Union's requirement to name a risk-owning authority has a 2029 deadline and a devolved answer. The pattern is now: an institution exists, a deadline is distant, the discretion is domestic, and the one line that moved this autumn moved downwards.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly publicly indispensable, and this week the compensation side acquired a number large enough to end the argument about scale. The loss and damage fund holds 822 million dollars pledged and about 450 million paid against 176 requests worth about 2.8 billion dollars, with 342 million reserved for a first round that covers roughly an eighth of what has been asked. The adaptation side was priced the same week at about 305 billion dollars a year needed by 2035 against 28 to 32 billion flowing. And the loss estimate for the week's own record rainfall event is a commercial forecaster's 3 to 5 billion dollars, with no public figure to set against it — the same structure as the European heat season. Indispensable assets are financeable before they break at a fifth of what is needed, and compensable after at an eighth of what is claimed.

The climate referent and the security register being decoupled by venue, and this week the decoupling turned out to have a geography rather than only a subject matter. A Union security body used the referent in a signed communique about the Sahel and the Lake Chad basin; the Union's own resilience law of nine days earlier contains no security institution anywhere. Meanwhile the three multilateral publications timed to the conference — adaptation finance, health, ocean observing — are security-relevant throughout and use no security vocabulary at all, reaching instead for finance, mortality and public goods. So the rule this trend has been feeling for is sharper than it was: the security register is available where the subject is other people's conflicts, and unavailable where the subject is one's own risk, one's own money or one's own instruments. That is not a vocabulary problem. It is a statement about who the field thinks climate insecurity happens to.

The contest is moving from the hazard to the apparatus that measures and prices it, and this week it reached the sensors. The ocean observing system's own status report records 67 contributing countries, 17 networks, 9,221 platforms and 890 observatories, with sustained implementation concentrated among the Group of Seven and Australia and the thinnest coverage over the Southern Ocean, the polar regions, the deep ocean and the coastal waters of developing countries and small island states. The organisation's secretary-general called it flying blind. Set against the same week's adaptation assessment — 305 billion needed, about 30 flowing, indicators cut from 100 to 59 at the last conference and still unimplemented — the apparatus is now contested on four axes: what the numbers are, who fixes the scenario, who certifies the assessment, and who owns the instruments. The fourth is the one with no venue. Nobody is negotiating the thermometers.

Forecast quality and institutional calendars have come apart, and this week two unconnected research communities proposed the same repair. A development researcher and a research-council specialist argued for pre-agreed triggers releasing climate money through regional risk pools and social protection systems, with hard deadlines — fourteen days for rapid finance after a declared sudden-onset disaster, about ninety days for recovery grant decisions — and public metrics on how long money takes to arrive. A fortnight earlier the director of a peace research institute's climate programme proposed one accountable body with a budget line plus pre-agreed finance released on forecast thresholds. The comparators now exist too: a regional pool and catastrophe bond due to pay Jamaica 242 million dollars within sixteen days, a regional insurer paying Vanuatu within fourteen, against a fund that took 57 days to set aside 21.6 million dollars and has disbursed nothing. The gap has money crossing it, a research description of why it exists, two independent designs for closing it, and still no published lead time.

The evidentiary question for climate loss is shifting from attribution to foreseeability, and this week the two futures this trend identified a fortnight ago acquired an institutional route out of the second one. Nepal and Bhutan have asked the conference to create a mountain work programme covering observation gaps, finance and adaptation assessment — which, if adopted, would make monitoring a multilateral obligation rather than a budget decision taken valley by valley. That is the only mechanism yet proposed that would prevent the funded basin's working alert chain from becoming the unfunded basin's best evidence in a liability claim. The attribution network published nothing this week on any event, including the Florida record, which leaves the foreseeability question where it has been: technically available, institutionally unowned.

Where displaced climate-security capacity goes. The three things this trend said to track are all unanswered after a fortnight. No second European-subject product from the American institute, whose climate tag has carried nothing since 29 October; no European institution has cited the first; and the foreign taskforce whose seat its director took has published nothing since its inaugural meeting. What the week adds is a different kind of destination, and it is not an institute. The field's reform thinking this week came from a development research council, an Australian university, a Lowy Institute commentary page and a Stockholm country fact sheet — none of them a climate-security institute, all of them doing what climate-security institutes used to do. The capacity may not be relocating to another institution at all. It may be dispersing into adjacent fields that never carried the security label.

open_threads.text: The Dutch institute's current funding phase. The route finally opened. After seven consecutive weeks of refused retrieval the platform's own site loaded this week, and what it shows is not a funding document but an answer to a different question: the platform states that it is powered by the Clingendael institute and gives a Dutch address, and every one of the seven items in its October news feed is somebody else's output — a Stockholm institute commentary on mine action and climate security posted on 28 October, an American institute's Gulf energy report, an Indian commentary, the Indian-Dutch South Asia report, a conflict-and-environment report, an alliance energy centre paper on radionuclides remobilised by wildfires and floods, and a peacebuilding film series. No funding information appears anywhere on the page. So the platform is a curation layer hosted by an institute, and the last publicly datable announcement of a funding phase remains December 2019. That is a stronger finding than seven refusals were, because the absence is now on a page that loads.

Whether the alliance published a fourth Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Still no, still no statement, and the displacing activity is now twenty-four days silent. Checked the climate centre of excellence's own site again this week: nothing from its Montreal summit of 15 and 16 October, against published recaps of the 2024 edition on 30 October 2024 and the 2025 edition on 15 October 2025. The week supplies one external contrast that makes the alliance's position harder to read as general practice rather than particular discipline: the Union's own security committee signed a document naming climate change as a driver of insecurity, in the same fortnight in which the alliance's binding resilience baselines remain the instrument from which the words were removed.

Whether the International Military Council's World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Tenth consecutive week of silence, and nothing from the Montreal meeting its secretary general was listed to speak at. The adjacent observation from a fortnight ago has not developed: the sister institute's European food security assessment of 29 October remains its latest climate item and no second European product has followed.
Funding trajectory of the joint United Nations climate security unit.
open_threads.resolution: Answered in magnitude, by a printed portfolio report rather than by the dashboard that has refused to render for three weeks. Cumulative deposits to the joint programme between 2016 and 2024 were $18.27 million, which places it thirteenth of fifteen funds in the trust fund office's climate and environment portfolio, against $808.89 million for the largest and about $2 million a year for this one. Fourteen governments contribute, eleven of them European; the Netherlands is not among them. The programme is not being wound down — a third phase runs 2026 to 2028 with ten advisers deployed — and it is funded at the level of a mid-sized national research grant. One consequence for this digest's own published record: Britain's £1 million of 25 September, reported here as three tenths of one per cent of a £331 million package and treated as a rounding error, is on the order of 5 per cent of everything this programme has ever received. The denominator was wrong. What remains unanswered is the year-by-year trajectory and whether the third phase has a stated requirement, which is carried forward as a separate question.

open_threads.text: Whether the 2028-2034 Union budget carries a security-tagged climate line. Unchanged, and the venue where it would now have to be created still has its date: a Council policy debate provisionally set for 11 December. One new adjacent fact worth holding against it. A Union security body signed a text this week naming climate change as a driver of insecurity in two African regions, with no money attached anywhere in the document. The referent arriving in Union security language without a line is the cheapest possible version of what this question was opened to look for, and it is what arrived first.

Chinese defence doctrine on climate. Twelfth week of nothing, and nothing dated inside this week from any Chinese security venue. The conference position, set out by a vice-minister of ecology and environment, is implementation, finance including a roadmap to the 300 billion dollar goal, and the free flow of green and low-carbon technologies, with a stated readiness to respond firmly to attacks — which locates the climate problem in market access, as it has all autumn. No head of government is attending the leaders' segment. The bilateral river mechanism with India produced nothing for a sixth week and the dry-season exchange is the next informative silence.

Any Indian security document on climate. Twelfth week of nothing, and this week the mis-specification this question has been accumulating evidence for was confirmed from the minister's own mouth. India's conference position asks for more adaptation finance as grants and simultaneously insists the global adaptation goal's indicators stay voluntary so they cannot condition access. That is a state defending sovereignty over the yardstick while accepting the money — the same instinct that funds six-figure evacuations through notified calamities with no security vocabulary attached. The three instruments that carry the file stand: the treaty expiry on 12 December, now 34 days away, the river mechanism with China, and the Delhi institute's argument about why South Asian climate cooperation does not happen. The committee route reconstituted on 26 September remains empty.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the loss and damage fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. Unchanged on the standard and transformed on the context, because the fund's delivery arithmetic was published this week: 822 million dollars pledged, about 450 million paid in, 176 requests worth about 2.8 billion dollars, 342 million reserved for a first round covering roughly an eighth of what is asked, nothing approved in the fund's first four years, and a first allocation that took 57 days. An appraisal regime is not the only thing missing; a throughput is missing. The December board in Manila on 15 December takes the long-term model including rapid disbursement, the commissioned lessons assessment and the first project approvals.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of national output to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment. Eighth checkpoint, and this week it is answered in the negative by something more solid than silence. The infrastructure and water budget was debated on 28 and 29 October — a correction to what this publication said a week ago — and the dominant subject was a cut, of 284 million euros to the freshwater line, with national co-financing for regional freshwater measures lapsing from 2027 and the minister saying the cut pains him while maintaining regional projects can proceed. A reprioritisation within the delta fund of about 250 million euros towards water quality was offered. None of that is new money and none of it touches the doubling. The water legislative session on 23 November is the next checkpoint and the first one with a stated date.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will receive it. Unchanged on adjudication; the administrative record keeps being built. The environment programme's assessment this week is organised around overshoot of 1.5 degrees as a condition to be prepared for rather than a limit to be argued about, which is the same move the Union's proposed law makes by fixing a three-degree planning path. Two institutions have now written the adaptation-limits premise into planning instruments. No fund board, bank, insurer or court has yet reasoned from it.

Who bears the privately held share of Nepal's losses, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. The numbers tightened this week and the answer got worse. The allocation is reported as 21.6 million dollars provisionally set aside on 22 October, which reconciles this publication's earlier 20 million plus 1.6 million of oversight fees as a single figure; nothing has been disbursed, no implementing organisation has been chosen because Nepal cannot apply directly, and the proposal is due at the board meeting of 15 December, by which point the flood will be 111 days old. Against a 4.8 billion dollar recovery estimate, with 2.7 billion of physical damage and economic loss, and against the fund's own 2.8 billion dollars of outstanding requests from other claimants.

Whether any security institution reads the September sea-level declaration as a security instrument. Still none, and the November programme makes it worse rather than merely unchanged. The Security Council's presidency for the month chose emerging technologies as its one signature debate, having taken maritime security and emerging technologies in October without touching the declaration, statehood continuity or maritime zones. Two consecutive discretionary slots, one of them maritime, and the first United Nations declaration on sea-level rise has not been mentioned in either.

Whether the alliance's removal of the climate referent from its binding resilience baseline is a drafting choice or standing practice. No new evidence from the alliance, and the centre of excellence that used the word freely on a programme page has now been silent for twenty-four days since the meeting where it used it. The week does supply the comparison that would discriminate between the two hypotheses if the alliance ever acts: the Union's security committee put the climate referent in a signed communique about Africa while the Union's internal resilience instrument carries no security institution. If removal were a general drafting discipline across Western security institutions, that communique should not exist.
Whether money reaches Somalia before the October-to-December rains.
open_threads.resolution: Answered yes, in part, and the answer required correcting this digest. Money did move before the rains: $7 million was pre-approved from the central emergency response fund in June for flood response preparedness ahead of the El Niño, alongside $10 million for drought response, and on 24 September Britain announced £5 million specifically for Deyr flood preparedness, split equally between a health, nutrition, water and protection programme led by Action Against Hunger and a Shabelle-basin rehabilitation programme delivered through three agencies, expected to reach about 600,000 people. Last week's digest said the money had not come; it had, one day before that was written. The proportions still carry the original finding: about £5 million and $7 million of anticipatory money against 2.5 to 3.5 million people exposed, roughly a million expected to be displaced, and a humanitarian plan at about a quarter funded. What happens next — whether the forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss — is carried forward as a new question rather than as this one.

open_threads.text: Whether India or China responds to Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, made from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September. Seventh week, still nothing from either capital, and this week Nepal stopped waiting. With Bhutan as co-sponsor it filed a supplementary agenda item for Antalya titled 1.5 degrees Celsius Warming in Mountains, carrying the same substance — observation, finance, adaptation assessment, an annual high-level dialogue, a dedicated work programme — into a venue where neither neighbour can decline to reply, only object on the record. The question therefore changes shape rather than closing: not whether Delhi or Beijing answers a bilateral proposal, but what either says at a plenary on 9 November when a mountain item is put to the room.

Whether the joint United Nations climate-security programme's third phase has a stated funding requirement, and whether contributions are rising, flat or falling. Unchanged and the route still not taken: the consolidated annual and financial reports for 2025 remain unopened. The unit's news stream has now been silent since 15 October, three and a half weeks, through the loudest pre-conference publishing week of the year. The denominator stands: 18.27 million dollars deposited from 2016 to 2024, which is less than a twentieth of what the loss and damage fund has been asked for and cannot pay.

Whether the climate panel remains the reference science for climate decisions, on what timetable, and which states are pressing on each axis. Sharpened by the conference's own framing of it. Delegations open the second global stocktake at Antalya without a certified assessment timetable, after a sixth consecutive failure to agree one; a majority want the three reports ready for the stocktake due in November 2028, with Saudi Arabia, India and Russia leading the smaller group arguing for later. Scientists are reported to be suggesting the conference's cover decision ask the panel to deliver its inputs on time, which would be the first time a political body has instructed the certification body on its own schedule. The resumed session is called for early December.

Whether any security institution treats the meteorological observing system's radio spectrum as an asset to be defended before the 2027 radiocommunication conference. Nothing again, and this week the question gained a sibling that may be the better route into it. The ocean observing system published a status report recording sustained implementation concentrated among the Group of Seven and Australia, with the thinnest coverage over the Southern Ocean, the polar regions, the deep ocean and developing-country coasts, and framed the problem as funding and governance — never as security or strategic dependency. Two classes of observing asset, both underwritten by a handful of states, both indispensable to every assessment, and no security institution has claimed an interest in either.

Whether any public institution produces an estimate of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost, to set against the private one. Answered no and retained because the structure keeps reproducing itself. This week the same pattern appeared on the other side of the Atlantic: the only total-loss figure for Florida's record rainfall is a commercial forecaster's preliminary 3 to 5 billion dollars, against a single city's public statement about roads and bridges. The Union's Climate Insurance Alliance is not due to deliver first measures until the end of 2027, so the insurer's 113 billion euro figure for the 2026 European season stands unopposed for at least another year.

Whether the Somali Deyr forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss. The first half continues to verify and the second half acquired an institutional observer this week without acquiring an answer. The Stockholm institute published a climate, peace and security fact sheet on Somalia dated November, by named researchers with a Norwegian institute co-author, which carries the forecast of wetter-than-usual conditions and high flood risk in central and southern Somalia for this October-to-December season and sets it against livelihood erosion, local resource conflict and political fragmentation, noting the national drought emergency declared in November 2025 after four failed seasons. It describes the exposure. Nobody has yet said who will measure whether the money reduced the loss, and the projection of 874,319 displaced between October and December stands.

Whether any candidate for Secretary-General states a position on climate, and in particular on Council competence over it. Nothing new. The November programme of work records that members are expected to continue straw polls through the month; no poll result and no candidate statement was found inside the week. Through six polls and the first use of colour-coded ballots, no candidate has been asked a public question about climate or about Council competence over it. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December, which gives this question seven weeks.
Whether the climate panel's plenary at Addis Ababa, 12 to 16 October, decides the timetable for its next assessment, and on which side.
open_threads.resolution: Answered, and the answer is neither of the two sides. The plenary did not decide. On the evening of Friday 16 October the chair, Jim Skea, suspended the session after it had run past its scheduled close and after delegations from least developed countries and small island developing states had left, rather than put the question to the room; the panel's statement says the timelines for the three working-group contributions and the panel's budget both "remain open" and that deliberations will resume "at the earliest opportunity", with no date given. Both subsidiary questions are answered the same way: the review of the panel's own principles and procedures was deferred for a further session, and nothing was decided about the budget, which is the item with a hard deadline because the 2027 budget depends on it and the panel must reconvene before the end of the year to set one. This was the sixth consecutive session to fail on the timetable, and the last scheduled before the November conference opens the second global stocktake's information phase. Around thirty countries pressed for all three reports by about September 2028; China, India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia are reported on the side of delivery in 2029 for the impacts and mitigation reports. The thread closes because its question had a date and the date has passed. Its successor is ipcc-resumed-session-budget, because the live question is no longer which side wins but whether the body can convene to decide at all.

open_threads.text: Whether the Union's reported position that there is no scope for new climate finance commitments at the November conference survives into adopted conclusions, and whether it holds at Antalya.
open_threads.resolution: The first half is answered and the answer is yes in substance and no in wording, which is the more interesting outcome. Environment ministers adopted the conclusions on 12 October as document 14250/26. The reported phrase does not appear. What appears instead is an absence: no new figure, no new instrument, no new pledge, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions approved by finance ministers on 9 October, a restatement of the New Collective Quantified Goal and the global goal of at least US$300 billion a year by 2035, support for at least tripling adaptation finance by 2035, and the record that developed countries provided and mobilised US$132.8 billion in 2023 and US$136.7 billion in 2024. A position that commits nothing does not have to say so. The second question — whether the extension of the mitigation work programme to at least 2040 was what the line was traded for — is answered in the negative and this digest had it wrong: the word 2040 does not appear anywhere in the adopted text, which asks only for the programme to be continued and strengthened. What was actually traded away was international carbon credits, removed from the innovative-finance list amid member-state disagreement about their place in the emissions trading system; only carbon pricing survives. The thread closes here rather than at Antalya because the mandate is now fixed and the conference will test it rather than the question. One sentence from the same document outlives the thread and is carried into section B instead: paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security".

open_threads.text: Whether the 1996 Ganges treaty is renewed, replaced or allowed to lapse, and on what terms. Thirty-four days to expiry as this week closes, and India's position is now on the record from its own ministry rather than inferred. At a briefing on 3 November the external affairs spokesperson, named in reporting as Randhir Jaiswal, said the two countries have an established mechanism for water-sharing discussions and that Bangladesh's prime minister has been invited to New Delhi. Bangladesh said on 29 October that India had not responded to its request to negotiate; at least one later account says discussions have formally begun. The three statements are not reconcilable from what is published and this publication asserts none of them. The load-bearing absence is unchanged: no study apportioning the Farakka dry-season decline between upstream abstraction and climate-driven hydrological change, which a guarantee clause would need.
Whether anyone publishes how much anticipatory climate money has actually disbursed, as against pledged.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved against this digest. The figure exists and has been public since 28 May 2026, in the fourth annual global overview of anticipatory action produced by the Anticipation Hub with the UN food and agriculture agency, the UN humanitarian coordination office, the humanitarian start network, the food programme, the German Red Cross, the international federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent societies, their climate centre and a German development agency. For 2025: anticipatory action triggered 146 times across 54 countries, almost US$120 million released, 9.6 million people directly reached, 262 active frameworks against 154 the year before, a further 205 frameworks in development across 71 countries, and 57 countries described as institutionalising the approach; Germany and the European Union named as the largest contributors among donors who supplied data; money for acting before a hazard reported separately from money for building the systems. Three caveats travel with it and none of them restores the thread: "released" is the report's own verb and is self-reported by the implementing organisations, there is no independent audit or counterfactual, and there is no breakdown of how far ahead of impact the money actually moved. That last is the successor question and it is now carried as anticipatory-lead-time-figure. For the record of what the figure means: almost US$120 million worldwide in a year is about US$12.50 per person reached, and roughly nine thousandths of one per cent of the US$1.3 trillion a year by 2035 that the November conference will argue about.

open_threads.text: Whether solar radiation modification's arrival in government climate-security forums is a one-off or the start of an agenda. Unchanged, and the institute that ran the Arctic tabletop has published nothing on its climate tag since 29 October. The foreign taskforce its director sits on has still published nothing. Eleven days on from the last item and three and a half weeks from the tabletop, there is no output and no government venue has taken the subject up.

Whether the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund reaches its 500 million dollar initial capitalisation target by the end of 2026. Nothing new inside the week, seven weeks left, and one development that changes what the fund is for rather than how much it holds: this week's loss and damage reform proposal names the Pacific Resilience Facility as one of the standing channels through which pre-agreed triggers should release money. If that design is adopted anywhere, a regional facility with a capitalisation total becomes a disbursement route with a function, which is a stronger position than a total. If it is not, a total without a route remains a total.

Whether 1 million US dollars is the going rate for Dutch climate-security and climate-resilience money, or a floor the Netherlands happened to set at one venue. No new Dutch number. What arrived instead is a foreign institute's grading that places the Netherlands among four European leaders on food-security climate resilience, which costs nothing, is worth more reputationally than the pledge, and sits oddly beside a country with no published adaptation strategy and no named risk owner.

Whether the climate panel reconvenes before the end of 2026, what it decides about its 2027 budget, and whether the budget and the assessment timetable are taken together. The session stands for early December, virtually, with the work plan and the trust fund budget as the only items. The new element is political rather than procedural: scientists are reported to be suggesting the Antalya cover decision ask the panel to deliver its inputs in time for the 2028 stocktake. That would route the timetable decision through the conference rather than the plenary, which is either a rescue of a body that cannot decide for itself or an instruction from the political process to the certification body, depending on how it is worded. The secretariat's estimate for completing the cycle is about 33 million Swiss francs and several 2027-2029 lines are unagreed.

Whether the forty-eight-day precursor signal on the slope above the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor is treated as foreseeability by any institution that has to decide something. Still none, and this week the only institutional movement on the underlying asymmetry came from the two governments with least leverage. Nepal and Bhutan's agenda item asks for a mountain work programme covering observation gaps, finance and adaptation assessment — which is the only proposal on the table that would make the difference between a monitored basin and an unmonitored one a multilateral obligation rather than a budget decision. The slope above the corridor is on the China-Nepal border and neither of those states co-sponsored the item.

Whether anyone publishes how far ahead of impact anticipatory money actually moves. Still nobody, and this week the question acquired the first proposal that would make the number mandatory. The loss and damage reform argument published on 6 November asks for public metrics on how long support takes to reach communities, alongside deadlines of fourteen days for rapid finance after a declared sudden-onset disaster and about ninety days for recovery grant decisions. It also supplies the comparators that make the absence embarrassing: a regional pool and catastrophe bond due to pay Jamaica 242 million dollars within sixteen days of a hurricane, and a regional insurer paying Vanuatu within fourteen days of an earthquake. Those are lead times. Nobody publishes one for the multilateral system.

Whether the first Dutch briefing on climate, nature and security is held during 2026, as a parliamentary motion asks. Seven weeks of the year left and nothing found. One thing did become clearer this week, from the defence ministry's own July letter: the defence climate strategy is named in it as the basis for that motion, so the briefing is formally downstream of a strategy whose action plan is four months overdue. And the chamber spent 4 and 5 November debating the climate budget without, on its own summary, any speaker raising climate security, defence or adaptation at all.

Whether the climate referent returns to a European Council conclusion in any substantive form. Not in a conclusion, and this week the institutional test returned an answer this question was not framed to expect. The referent appeared in a Union security text — a joint communique signed by the Council's standing Political and Security Committee, naming the adverse impacts of climate change as a driver of insecurity in the Sahel and committing to address them in the Lake Chad basin. Nine days after a resilience law containing no security institution. So the referent is now in Union law and in Union security language, and the two are about different continents. The question worth carrying forward is narrower and sharper than the original: whether a Union security body will ever use it about Europe.

Whether the loss and damage fund's 20 million dollar ceiling for a single project and its out-of-cycle submission route become stated policy, and at what level. Unchanged as policy and newly contextualised by the fund's own arithmetic, published this week: 176 requests worth about 2.8 billion dollars, 342 million reserved for the first round, 822 million pledged and about 450 million actually paid in. A ceiling is what a fund uses when demand is eight times supply, which is roughly the ratio. The board meets in Manila on 15 December with the long-term model, the lessons assessment and the first approvals.

Whether the projected tropical Pacific anomaly of up to 3.8 degrees for November to January verifies, and whether any security institution acts on the forecast before the peak. On the second question, seven weeks and still nothing: no defence ministry, alliance body or security council has said anything about it, and the Security Council's November programme carries no climate item in any framing. On the first, the weekly central Pacific reading has reached 3.4 degrees above average, the highest of this event, with the peak expected around December and the federal prediction centre's next monthly discussion due on 12 November. Two different indices are in circulation and give different answers to the record question, so any claim that this is the strongest event since 1950 has to say which one it is using.

Whether the British climate and nature security taskforce produces anything, by when, and whether any of it reaches a spending document. Nothing published, now nineteen days from its inaugural meeting, which remains consistent with a body given up to two meetings in 2026 and no reporting date. The spending-document test stands for a body of this kind.

Whether 'illegal exploitation of natural resources' becomes the Security Council's standing frame for resources and conflict. Answered in part this week, and from the continental rather than the global Council. Both sides proposed an agenda item on the role of natural resource exploitation in conflicts for the African Union and Union joint consultative meeting, and it was dropped — yet the formulation appears in the adopted communique anyway, in the eastern Congo paragraph, condemning the illegal exploitation of natural resources by all armed groups and other actors. So the frame now travels without an agenda item, which makes it a conflict-economy description rather than the resource governance agenda this question opened on. It has not reappeared in a Security Council product; that Council's November programme carries no resources item at all.

Whether any government creates a body that is accountable for the gaps between its climate-security silos and gives it a budget line. No government has, and this week the proposition acquired a second independent advocate from an unconnected literature. Development researchers argued for pre-agreed triggers releasing climate money through regional pools and national systems, with hard deadlines and published delivery metrics — the forecast-threshold half of the ownership argument put from a development research position rather than a peace research one. The institutional half remains adopted at Union level in form and declined in money: twenty-seven capitals must name risk-owning authorities by June 2029, with no funding attached and the choice of body devolved. The countable question is unchanged: which body each capital names, and whether any of the twenty-seven names a defence, interior or security body.

Whether the proposed European Climate Resilience Law reaches adoption with its two load-bearing provisions intact: the mandatory reference warming trajectory and the duty on each member state to name public authorities responsible for each major climate risk. It is in the Council's working party on the environment; parliamentary treatment is expected in 2027 and a Council policy debate is provisionally set for 11 December. The attack lines are now visible from both flanks: the largest parliamentary group's lead negotiator has questioned whether the plans are needed in their current form, the Greens say the law commits to nothing, and environmental groups say its nature-based solutions language carries no targets or funding. The insurance industry's European federation wants the planning duty and is sceptical of the single Union-wide scenario, which is the pairing that would, if it prevailed, remove the premise and keep the paperwork.

Whether the African group's three requested agenda items reach the provisional agenda and survive its adoption at the opening of the Antalya conference. The answer falls on 9 November, the day after this week closes. Two things sharpened in the final week. The group's own chair is reported as saying nobody is sure what the tripling baseline is and that the pathways are unclear, which is the substantive case for an item rather than a procedural one; and the trade item is now described as aiming to tie existing trade dialogues into formal negotiations within two years, with European pushback expected, which is the association that could sink the finance item. A second supplementary request has also arrived, from Nepal and Bhutan on mountains, so the opening plenary now has at least four contested items rather than three.

How the Bhutan-to-India glacial-hazard alert of 30 October actually travelled, and whether anything equivalent exists on the Nepal-China border. Still undescribed by any of the three institutions that could describe it, and this week the question gained significance rather than an answer. Bhutan is the co-sponsor of Nepal's mountain agenda item, which is a choice of partner: the state whose alert chain worked is now the state lending its name to a proposal for a multilateral mountain work programme covering observation and early warning. The working example is doing diplomatic work while remaining technically unexplained.

Whether the environment programme's 2026 adaptation assessment was in fact published on 28 October, and if so why no launch, coverage or readable text can be found for it. The programme's own publication listing carries the date; its site would not open on any attempt, no press release was found, and no news coverage of the 2026 edition's contents exists. The emissions report of 21 October got a launch and set the numbers every delegation will quote at Antalya; the adaptation report, which is where the security-relevant finance gap lives, appears to have had none. Datable: whether the text becomes readable before the conference opens, and whether any delegation cites a 2026 figure from it.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved, and against this publication. The report was not published on 28 October and was not buried. It was launched on 4 November 2026 as *Ready? Not*, with a media statement from the environment programme's executive director, a UN News lead, a dedicated insights event and wide pickup, five days before the Antalya conference opened — the most prominent slot of the year. The 28 October date was a catalogue entry for a publication still under embargo, and the absence of launch materials a week earlier was the absence of a launch that had not happened yet. The substance is in section B: about 305 billion dollars a year of need by 2035 against 28.2 to 31.7 billion of international public adaptation finance in 2024, tripling reaching 20 to 29 per cent of need after inflation, and 49 to 83 per cent for least developed countries and small island states. The one finding this question was opened to look for survives in a different form: the report where the security-relevant finance gap should live contains no conflict, fragility, security, displacement or migration axis at all, on every route that opened. That absence is carried forward as its own question. The inference error is treated in this week's pushback, because it is a lesson about evidence rather than a slip.

open_threads.text: Whether the finding that national governments, international organisations and the private sector are disengaging from climate and health is corroborated by any independent measure. Unchanged in substance and worth noting against the week's one apparently contrary data point: the health organisation published a costed six-measure climate and health package on 4 November, which is engagement rather than disengagement from one international organisation. Whether that cuts against the finding or is exactly the advocacy response the finding would predict cannot be decided from a single publication. The indicator series behind the original claim remains the route to a check.

Whether the field's authoritative adaptation finance assessment ever acquires a fragility axis. The 2026 edition prices the gap at about 305 billion dollars a year of need against 28 to 32 billion flowing, and organises the shortfall by instrument, flow and institutional barrier. Conflict, fragility, security, displacement and migration do not appear as categories on any route that opened. The relationship is measurable and has been measured: across 133 countries from 2000 to 2022 conflict weakens the link between climate vulnerability and climate finance for both mitigation and adaptation, while strong recipient institutions strengthen it. So the assessment that sets the field's numbers is missing a variable that the peer-reviewed literature says governs its own distribution. Three places an answer could appear: the 2027 edition's framing, the conference's adaptation indicator work, and whether any delegation at Antalya cites a fragility-adjusted need figure.

Whether a Union security body ever uses the climate referent about Europe. This week the Council's standing Political and Security Committee signed a communique naming the adverse impacts of climate change as a driver of insecurity in the Sahel and committing to address them in the Lake Chad basin — the first instance this publication has found of the referent inside a signed Union security text. Nine days earlier the Commission published a resilience law containing no security or defence institution anywhere. The decoupling this publication has tracked by venue therefore has a geography: the security register is available for other people's conflicts and unavailable for Europe's own risk. Observables: whether any member state's eventual designation of a risk-owning authority names a security, defence or interior body; whether the external action service's climate-security work appears in an internal instrument; and whether a Council security product ever names a European climate hazard as a security matter.

Whether anyone treats the concentration of the world's climate observing capacity as a strategic dependency. The ocean observing system's own 2026 status report records 67 contributing countries but sustained implementation concentrated among the Group of Seven and Australia, with the thinnest coverage over the Southern Ocean, the polar regions, the deep ocean and the coastal waters of developing countries and small island states, and frames the problem entirely as funding and governance. Adjacent analysis published earlier in 2026 found that losing United States-funded platforms would sharply increase errors in ocean warming estimates, and European float deployments have been falling on cost grounds. This is the sibling of the standing question about the meteorological radio spectrum: two classes of indispensable observing asset, both underwritten by a handful of states, and no security institution claiming an interest in either.

Whether any security institution updates the number under the threat-multiplier claim. The 2013 meta-analysis that made this literature quantitative reported a 14 per cent rise in intergroup conflict risk per standard deviation of climate change; three of its four authors published a revised meta-analysis in 2024, with the usable study pool raised from 30 to 80 and pre-1960 historical studies excluded, giving 2.5 per cent — roughly three quarters smaller — while concluding that the association itself should now be treated as a robust empirical fact. A decade of defence and foreign-ministry documents rests on the older figure. The datable observables are specific: whether the revised coefficient appears in the climate panel's next assessment, in any alliance or national climate-security document, or in the African Union's commissioned study on climate-related security risks.

Whether the Nepal and Bhutan request for a mountain agenda item at Antalya is adopted, diverted or refused, and what India and China say about it. The item, titled 1.5 degrees Celsius Warming in Mountains and filed under rule 12, asks for a scientific assessment of overshoot consequences in mountain regions, an annual high-level dialogue, a dedicated convention work programme on mountain ecosystems, and mountain-specific treatment in adaptation, finance and loss and damage. It is the Himalayan resilience mechanism Nepal proposed in September, redirected into a venue where its two large neighbours cannot simply not reply. The answer to the first part falls on 9 November; the answer to the second may not be given in public at all, which is itself the finding to look for.

open_moves.text: Denmark's Security Council food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Closed as not produced. October has ended: the month's programme carried no food-security item in any framing, the only remaining route — the joint seminar with the African Union on 22 October — took illegal exploitation of natural resources instead, and the month closed on 30 October with three mandate renewals, two failed drafts on Western Sahara and an open debate on maritime security and emerging technologies. No outcome document traceable to the debate has ever appeared. A famine risk was classified in Somalia during the month and no Council member raised it.

open_moves.text: The American climate-security institute's philanthropic-funding bet. Checked its own climate tag, which is the route that carried its recent items: nothing since the European food security assessment of 29 October, eleven days. Its homepage is reported as carrying a 2 November post on artificial intelligence under the centre's heading, credited to a different lab within the same organisation, which does not appear on the climate tag and is not counted here as climate research. The register observation from October therefore stands and the volume question is unresolved: one climate product in six weeks, and the customer for it was European.

The Abyei climate, peace and security report and the next peacekeeping mandate renewal. Two findings this week, one of them a correction to this digest's method. The Stockholm institute's climate-change-and-security publications list still ends at the August Abyei study, checked again this week — but the institute published a commentary on integrating mine action into climate security on 6 October which does not appear on that list and surfaced only because another platform carried it on 28 October. So the list is not the institute's output and should not be read as a silence detector; that correction has been made to the standing roster. On the renewal: the mandates decided on 30 October were Colombia, the European force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Libya, with two drafts on Western Sahara failing. None is Abyei, and no climate language was found in the three adopted texts as reported.
PIF security-declaration merger.

The Union's climate resilience framework, announced in the State of the Union address of 16 September. Delivered on 27 October, a day earlier than reporting of the pre-briefing had it, and the pre-briefing was substantially right: a hundred most-vulnerable territories to be identified, named risk owners to be designated by member states, a three-degree reference point for planning, and no ring-fenced money, with adaptation tied to the long-term budget negotiation. What the pre-briefing did not convey is the form — a proposed regulation with a mandatory reference warming trajectory and thirteen mandatory planning areas, water security among them — or the timetable, which runs to national plans by the end of 2030. Superseded by D2 on the ownership question and by the new thread on the law's passage.

open_moves.text: Succession to the Secretary-General. No seventh straw poll result and no new entry or withdrawal found inside the week. The November programme of work records that members are expected to continue straw polls through the month. The finding is unchanged through six polls and the first use of colour-coded ballots: no candidate has been asked a public question about climate or about Council competence over it. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December.

The Turkish presidency of the Antalya conference, 9 to 20 November, with Australia running the negotiations. The final pre-conference week fixed the architecture. The opening plenary on 9 November faces at least four contested supplementary items — the African group's three and the Nepal and Bhutan mountain item — and Australia is reported as wanting to avoid an agenda fight. The leaders' segment is 11 and 12 November with a low-key speaker list and neither India nor China sending heads of government. The flagship is a voluntary electrification pledge launching on 10 November, committing signatories to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035 from about 23 to 24 per cent now, against a current-policy projection of about 28 per cent; it does not specify clean power, which the Union wants and India is reported as rejecting outright. Both presidencies plan a cover decision, and whether it may cite the outgoing presidency's fossil fuel roadmap is unresolved. Two structural facts carry in: the second global stocktake begins here, and the panel that certifies its science has no agreed assessment timetable.

Whether overshoot is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Advanced quietly and in the Union's own adopted text: the conclusions of 12 October reiterate the aim of "bringing the temperature increase to or below 1.5C by the end of the century", which is overshoot language adopted as a negotiating position without being described as such, drawing on the UN environment programme's report of 2 October. No security institution has adopted the premise, which is the original question and still unanswered.
open_moves.resolution: Completed, and promoted. What was a spotlight report on limiting overshoot on 2 September is now the headline of the programme's flagship pre-conference document: the Emissions Gap Report 2026, subtitled The Point of Return, treats exceeding 1.5°C as virtually unavoidable and reframes the objective as minimising the peak and the duration and returning below the limit by 2100. The move landed. What it did not carry with it is any treatment of adaptation, adaptation limits, loss and damage or security, in any of the published readings.

open_moves.text: The small island states' refusal of the overshoot frame. Still not restated; the most recent statement found remains 21 September. This week makes the silence harder to read as tactical patience. The environment programme published an assessment organised around overshoot as a condition to prepare for, titled as a question about readiness, which prices the tripling these states are negotiating for at 49 to 83 per cent of their own need — the most favourable number in the report and the one that would most repay an alliance statement. None came.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data wall. Advanced this week by diplomacy rather than engineering. Nepal and Bhutan's mountain agenda item asks for a convention work programme covering mountain observation gaps, which is the first proposal that would fund monitoring as a multilateral obligation rather than basin by basin. It does not address the data wall: the slope above the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor is on the China-Nepal border and neither China nor India co-sponsored the item.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. Closed as an episode. Nothing has revived it in eight weeks, and Nepal's posture through that period has been outward-facing in every direction: a sovereign claim before the loss and damage fund, a regional mechanism proposed from the Assembly rostrum, and a joint cross-border scientific mission. The restriction was a decision taken in the first week of a disaster and not a doctrine.
