open_moves.text: Whether the climate convention secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any European security institution adopts the formulation.
open_moves.resolution: Answered on both halves and not in the way the question expected. A European security institution did adopt a security framing: on 24 September the Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks. But it adopted this field's own formulation, national security risk, not the secretariat's economic-security substitution. And the secretary himself substituted again in the same week, telling Climate Week that electrification shields countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and calling it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy — security fourth, and meaning supply security. So the two moved past each other: the institution reached for the field's register in the same week the secretariat reached past it. The question is closed because its premise has been falsified. It assumed the secretariat's phrasing would be the vector by which the security frame travelled into European institutions, and the frame travelled without it.

open_moves.text: Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent ask converts into any government commitment. Seventh checkpoint and the first with hard evidence rather than silence, and the evidence runs the other way. The infrastructure and water budget was debated on 28 and 29 October — which this publication wrongly placed later in the autumn — and its dominant subject was a 284 million euro cut to the delta programme's freshwater line, with national co-financing for regional freshwater measures lapsing from 2027. About 250 million euros of reprioritisation within the delta fund towards water quality was offered. Neither is new money. The water legislative session on 23 November is the next dated checkpoint.

Nepal's claim on the loss and damage fund for the August cascade. The figure is now reported as a single 21.6 million dollars provisionally set aside on 22 October, which reconciles the 20 million plus 1.6 million of oversight fees this publication carried separately. Nothing disbursed, no implementing organisation chosen because Nepal cannot apply directly, proposal due at the 15 December board in Manila, by which point the flood will be 111 days old. Against 2.7 billion dollars of physical damage and economic loss, a 4.8 billion dollar recovery estimate, and a toll reported this week as at least 1,455 dead and 5,285 missing in Nepal with 43 dead and 519 missing on the Chinese side.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether the alliance ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual climate and security assessment. Still no statement, and the displacing event is now twenty-four days unreported by either host. Checked the centre of excellence's own site again this week; nothing new. Against published recaps of the 2024 edition on 30 October 2024 and the 2025 edition on 15 October 2025, the contrast is now a full month wide.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it. Eight weeks, and no fund board, bank, insurer or court has reasoned from adaptation limits. The premise continues to enter planning instruments instead: the environment programme's assessment this week is built on overshoot of 1.5 degrees as a condition to prepare for, as the Union's proposed law is built on a three-degree reference path. The attribution network published nothing at all this week, including on the Florida record.
Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern.
open_moves.resolution: Answered no, and closed. Four consecutive weeks with no new state-level briefer since Ohio on 18 September; no state government named as commissioner or partner on any of the five; no second American institute writing for statehouses; and the institute's new programme capacity going elsewhere twice over — the parent's fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security, applications closing 20 October, and the institute's own event of 27 October on electric vehicles as defence technology. The statehouse series was one bet among several and it is not the one being pressed. The successor question is not where American climate-security work relocates geographically but which register it survives in, and on this month's evidence the answer is technology and supply-chain competition with China. That is carried by the csr-ccs-staffing move rather than as a new thread.

open_moves.text: Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's response to the 2027 delta programme and the autumn estimates. Answered, and against the softer reading. The infrastructure and water budget debate of 28 and 29 October was dominated by a planned 284 million euro cut to the freshwater line, with national co-financing for regional freshwater measures lapsing from 2027; the minister said the cut pains him and that regional projects can proceed anyway. Members of four parties pressed on drought and on water framework targets. The flood-protection programme and water quality were also debated, with about 250 million euros of reprioritisation within the delta fund offered towards water quality. So the asymmetry was confirmed in writing, in a debate this publication reported as still ahead. The final adaptation strategy and the national implementation programme, promised for December, are where it would have to be corrected.

The British, European and Kenyan foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, 24 September. Six weeks on, no institutional follow-through from any of the three — but the Union's external action service is no longer absent from the file. Its managing director for Africa attended the joint consultative meeting of 6 November at which the Union's security committee signed a communique naming climate change as a driver of insecurity in the Sahel and the Lake Chad basin. That is the service's first appearance in a climate-referent security text since this move opened, and it is on the external file.

The British climate security package of September 2026. Unchanged: the taskforce has published nothing since its inaugural meeting and the membership release of 21 October, and it has up to two meetings in 2026, no reporting date, no budget and no measurable target. Nineteen days.

Nepal's proposal, from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September, for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China. Seventh week, no response from either capital, and this week Nepal changed venue rather than waiting. With Bhutan it filed a supplementary agenda item for Antalya titled 1.5 degrees Celsius Warming in Mountains, carrying the same substance into a forum where the two neighbours must either object on the record or let it proceed. The bilateral proposal is not withdrawn and is not answered; it has been overtaken by its own author.

The alliance's revision and first public release of its seven baseline requirements for resilience, 15 September. Nothing new from the alliance. The pattern this move documented — a hazard referent present in analysis, absent from instruments — acquired a genuine counter-example this week from the other Western security architecture: the Union's Political and Security Committee signed a text naming climate change as a driver of insecurity. That makes the alliance's omission from its binding baselines look more like particular drafting discipline and less like a bloc-wide convention, which is the narrower and more testable reading.

Australia's Climate Week keynote on climate security as national security, 21 September, and the challenge to it from a former chief of defence asking where the plan is. Nothing new from the minister in that register. He runs the negotiations at Antalya, where his team is reported as wanting to avoid an agenda fight on 9 November — which is the opposite posture to the keynote's, and a fair measure of how little the security framing travels into the chair.

Fiji's four-pillar position for the pre-conference talks, set out on 29 September. Nothing new inside the week. The regional declaration of 6 October is the position that travels to Antalya and the science pillar remains untransacted: the body it was aimed at still has no agreed assessment timetable, and the route now being suggested for fixing that is the conference's own cover decision rather than the panel's plenary.

The American climate-security institute's private tabletop on the security dynamics of a fictional 2030 stratospheric aerosol deployment, 14 October. No output, no participants named, and nothing on the institute's climate tag since 29 October. Its conclusions remain the thing to watch for adoption and no government venue has taken the subject up.

Greece's Security Council programme of work for October, announced 1 October. Closed with the month. The finding held to the last day: no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing across the whole month. What the presidency ran instead was the succession, including the first colour-coded straw poll in the process's history on 16 October, a joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October that took illegal exploitation of natural resources, and a closing week of three mandate renewals, two failed drafts on Western Sahara and an open debate on maritime security and emerging technologies that did not mention sea-level rise.

open_moves.text: The Berlin climate and security conference of 6 October, hosted by the German foreign ministry with the institute that founded it. Open on the only question the format leaves — whether any defence ministry repeats the weaponisation claim — and nothing this week repeated it. The alliance climate centre's note on the 2025 edition still has no 2026 equivalent.

The presidency's pricing of the climate finance ask against the alliance's defence commitment, made at the Nadi pre-conference talks on 8 October. Reported in detail in late October: asked whether countries should spend as much on climate as on defence, the president-designate answered much more, said the climate issue is the security issue itself, and urged alliance members to exceed their 5 per cent commitment with climate spending. The comparison is still rhetorical on the presidency's side and fiscal on the other: one European government will deliver half its pledge to the main climate fund because it is spending more on security, two others have cut aid, and the fund has written its first rules for non-sovereign money. This week's adaptation assessment prices what the rhetoric would have to cover — about 305 billion dollars a year by 2035.
The Union's draft negotiating position for the November conference, reported on 6 October from a copy seen by a financial wire, stating there is no scope for new climate finance commitments.
open_moves.resolution: Landed, in substance and not in wording. The conclusions were adopted by environment ministers in Luxembourg on 12 October as document 14250/26 under the Irish presidency, chaired by climate minister Darragh O'Brien. The reported phrase is not in the text; what is in the text is an absence of any new commitment, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions of 9 October, and a restatement of existing goals. The expected trade did not happen: the word 2040 appears nowhere, and the mitigation work programme is only to be continued and strengthened. What was traded away was international carbon credits, deleted from the innovative-finance list; only carbon pricing survives. Two things from the same document outlive this move and are carried forward instead. Its paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security". And its paragraph 11 condemns Russia's war of aggression and reiterates concern about the Middle East, in the strategic framing of a climate mandate, with nothing joining either to anything climatic — which is the current limit of what the Union will assert, in a text revised five times.

open_moves.text: The loss and damage fund's board called the first extraordinary meeting in its existence, for 22 October, on a draft decision provisionally setting aside US$20 million for Nepal and piloting a route for requests outside the fund's regular call for proposals.
open_moves.resolution: Held and decided. The board agreed unanimously to set aside 20 million dollars for Nepal plus 1.6 million in administrative and oversight fees — which settles last week's small question: the fees sit on top of the allocation, not inside it — and invited Nepal to submit a proposal for a later meeting. Nothing has been disbursed. The out-of-cycle route was used and then disowned as a precedent by three contributing governments; see D4. The decision text, by the only account that read it, says nothing about the standard of evidence a claim from an unattributed event must meet.

open_moves.text: The panel's chair suspended the sixty-fifth plenary on 16 October rather than decide without the delegations that had gone home, and the session is called back for early December, virtually. The suspension's cost is now visible in the conference's own agenda: delegations open the second global stocktake at Antalya without a certified assessment timetable, after a sixth consecutive failure, and scientists are reported to be suggesting the cover decision instruct the panel to deliver in time for the 2028 stocktake.

An Indian institute's workshop report with a Dutch partner, published 12 October, arguing that shared climate vulnerability in South Asia does not produce collective action because governance is national and siloed, sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities constrain what can be proposed, and asymmetries make states facing one hazard set different priorities. This week is a second test and the report passes it. Nepal's bilateral proposal to India and China has gone unanswered for seven weeks; Nepal's new coalition for the same substance is Bhutan, Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan — four states with no capacity to deliver it and no sovereignty objection to raising it. The report's own logic predicts exactly that substitution.

The alliance's climate centre convened the Montreal climate security summit on 15 and 16 October, by invitation, on how to spend the climate-relevant share of a rising defence budget. Twenty-four days on, neither host has published anything. Checked the centre's own site again this week. The thing to watch remains procurement metrics rather than communiques, because climate-resilience metrics for defence procurement is the instrument that would let a treasury book resilience spending against both ledgers.

The Security Council's first use of colour-coded ballots in a straw poll on the succession, on 16 October. No seventh poll result found inside the week; the November programme says polls are expected to continue. The only question that matters here is unchanged: whether anyone asks any candidate a public question about climate or about Council competence over it before the choice is made.

A British department published the membership of the first standing ministerial climate and nature security taskforce and held its inaugural meeting on 21 October. Nothing published since, nineteen days. Open until it publishes something or a recommendation of its appears in a spending document.

The director of the Swedish peace research institute's climate programme argued on 22 October that climate security's problem is ownership rather than coordination, attacked the threat-multiplier formulation as naming no mechanism, and proposed one accountable central body with a budget line plus pre-agreed finance released on forecast thresholds. Two weeks later the forecast-threshold half arrived independently from an unconnected literature: development researchers writing for an Australian institute proposed pre-agreed triggers releasing loss and damage money through regional risk pools and social protection systems, with fourteen- and ninety-day deadlines and published delivery metrics. Two research communities, no shared institutions, same design. The institutional half remains adopted at Union level in form and declined in money. One footnote on the attack on the threat-multiplier formulation: this week's section A shows the number under it has been cut by about three quarters by the people who produced it, which strengthens the complaint about mechanism from an unexpected direction.

The conference's president of negotiations named five ministerial pairs to facilitate mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and ocean, with no pair for loss and damage. The first test falls on 9 November, when the opening plenary meets at least four contested supplementary items. One more absence from that list is now visible: the health organisation published a costed six-measure climate and health package into a conference with no health pair either.

Germany, Czechia and Japan placed on the record that the fund's first allocation sets no precedent and is truly exceptional, against Pakistan's and Ecuador's attempts to make it learnable; the board did commission a lessons assessment. This week's published arithmetic shows what the no-precedent position is protecting: 176 requests worth about 2.8 billion dollars against 822 million pledged and about 450 million paid, with 342 million reserved for a first round. A precedent at 21.6 million dollars per disaster, applied to the queue, is a bill none of the three has budgeted for. Unchanged until the 15 December board in Manila.

Ghana, chairing the African Group of Negotiators, wrote to the climate convention's executive secretary asking for three new Antalya agenda items — tripling adaptation finance, trade and climate change, and the main climate fund's financing arrangements. No other developing-country bloc had formally backed it as the week closed. Two refinements from the final week: the group's chair is reported as saying nobody is sure what the tripling baseline is and that the pathways are unclear, and the trade item is described as aiming to tie existing trade dialogues into formal negotiations within two years, with European pushback expected. Open until the conference adopts its agenda on 9 November, which is a hard date.

Presenting the proposed Climate Resilience Law, the climate commissioner created a duty on member states to name one or more public authorities responsible for each major climate risk and said explicitly that where that responsibility sits is for member states to decide. The proposal is now in the Council's working party on the environment with a policy debate provisionally set for 11 December and parliamentary treatment expected in 2027. The countable question is unchanged: whether any of the twenty-seven names a security, defence or interior body. This week gives it a sharper edge, because the Union's own security committee has now shown it will use the climate referent — about Africa.

The American climate-security institute published its first climate research in a month and the subject was European food security and climate resilience, by a Europe-based visiting researcher, two days after the Commission's package and engaging it directly. Eleven days on, no second European-subject product and no European institution has cited the first. Checked the institute's climate tag this week.

A secretariat letter on the chair's behalf called the suspended sixty-fifth plenary back for early December, to be held virtually, with the assessment work plan and the trust fund budget as the only remaining items. Open until the session sits. The format is still the part to judge, and the week adds a second route to the same decision: the Antalya cover decision may be asked to instruct the panel on its own delivery, which would make the political process the venue for a question the panel has failed six times to settle itself.

The main climate fund's board adopted an updated contributions policy for its third replenishment and its first policy for contributions from sources other than sovereign donors, reappointing its executive director in the same meeting. Open until a contribution under the new policy is named and its source disclosed. This week's adaptation assessment supplies the pressure the policy anticipates: private flows are estimated to close only 15 to 20 per cent of the publicly oriented adaptation gap, so non-sovereign money is a supplement to a shortfall rather than a substitute for it.

Nepal and Bhutan filed a supplementary agenda item for the Antalya conference, titled 1.5 degrees Celsius Warming in Mountains, under rule 12 of the draft rules of procedure: a scientific assessment of overshoot consequences in mountain regions, an annual high-level dialogue, a dedicated convention work programme on mountain ecosystems, and mountain-specific treatment in adaptation, finance and loss and damage. It is the substance of Nepal's unanswered September proposal to India and China, moved to a venue where neither can decline to reply. Open until the opening plenary of 9 November adopts, diverts or refuses it.

Latvia's Security Council presidency adopted a November programme whose single signature event is a high-level open debate on emerging technologies and security, with no climate, water, food security, environment or natural resources item anywhere on it, one year after this Council met formally on climate and security in the same month. Open on whether the unannounced high-level briefing of 23 November carries any climate content, which is the month's one remaining discretionary slot.

Cote d'Ivoire's chairmanship of the African Union Peace and Security Council scheduled a session for 11 November on climate, peace and security in Africa, after the September session on the same theme was postponed, to report on February's decisions including a study on climate-related security risks and possibly to update on a common African position. Open until the session sits, and then on whether either document exists.

Two researchers, one at an Australian university and one at Canada's development research centre, argued three days before the conference that the loss and damage fund's constraint is speed rather than size, and proposed pre-agreed triggers through regional risk pools and social protection systems, fourteen-day and ninety-day decision deadlines, published delivery metrics and a hub-and-spoke architecture. It is the second independent arrival of the forecast-trigger design in a fortnight. Open until any board, fund or government adopts a trigger or a deadline.

India's environment minister fixed the country's conference position on 3 November: commence the climate finance work programme, finance as a treaty obligation and predominantly public, concessional and non-debt-creating, adaptation finance as grants, and the global adaptation goal's indicators voluntary so they cannot condition access to finance. Open until the conference closes on 20 November, and specifically on whether the voluntary-indicator position survives into the adaptation decision.
